chapters.name: Chapter 1: Know your options and where to find them

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Apprenticeship, pre-apprenticeship or training program?
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Identify the three main kinds of programs and which one fits you now.
This lesson builds toward: Given short descriptions of five programs, you will identify each one as an apprenticeship, a pre-apprenticeship or a job training program, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
A Registered Apprenticeship is a job. The US Department of Labor's apprenticeship.gov says apprentices earn a wage from day one, get raises as their skills grow, learn on the job with classroom training, and finish with a credential recognized across their industry. You apply to the employer or program sponsor, much like a job.
A pre-apprenticeship gets you ready for an apprenticeship. Apprenticeship.gov says it can last a few weeks to a few months, and pay or a stipend is optional. It often covers basic math, safety and job readiness. YouthBuild is one example for young people.
A job training program teaches skills for a job, often in a classroom, and helps you find work at the end. Examples are Job Corps, community college certificates, and training paid for through your local American Job Center. Some are free; some help with costs; you are usually not paid a wage while you learn.
Ask yourself: do I need to earn money now (apprenticeship), do I need to get ready first (pre-apprenticeship), or do I need a short course to qualify for a job (training program)?
Words to know:
- Registered Apprenticeship: a paid job with training, approved by the Department of Labor or a state, that ends with a recognized credential.
- Pre-apprenticeship: a short program that prepares you to get into an apprenticeship.
- Sponsor: the employer, union or group that runs an apprenticeship and hires the apprentices.
- Stipend: a small payment to help with costs while you train; it is not a full wage.
- Credential: proof of a skill, such as a certificate or license.
Official sources:
- Apprenticeship.gov: Career seekers
- Apprenticeship.gov: What is a pre-apprenticeship?
- US Department of Labor: YouthBuild
Try it now: On paper, make three columns: Apprenticeship, Pre-apprenticeship, Training program. Write two good things and one hard thing about each for YOUR life right now. Circle the one that fits you best today.
You can now tell an apprenticeship, a pre-apprenticeship and a job training program apart and pick the kind that fits you now.

check.q: Which program pays you a wage while you learn on the job?
check.why: A Registered Apprenticeship is a paid job with training.

check.q: A 10-week program teaches construction math and safety to help you get into an apprenticeship. What is it?
check.why: A pre-apprenticeship prepares you to enter an apprenticeship and can last weeks to months.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Searching the apprenticeship.gov Job Finder
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Search the official Job Finder and write down two apprenticeship listings near you.
This lesson builds toward: Using the apprenticeship.gov Job Finder on a phone or computer, you will search for apprenticeships in your field and area and write down two listings, with the sponsor, location and how to apply for each.
Apprenticeship.gov is the US Department of Labor's official apprenticeship site. Its Apprenticeship Job Finder lets you type a career path or a location to find openings near you.
The Job Finder pulls listings from several sources. Each listing has a tag such as "Registered Occupation" or "Registered Partner". You apply directly with the employer or sponsor, not through apprenticeship.gov.
Try more than one word: "electrician", "plumber", "IT support", "medical assistant", "truck driver". Apprenticeships are not only in construction; they are also in health care, IT, manufacturing and more. If you find nothing nearby, try a bigger city near you or a different job title.
Write down what you find before you close the page. Listings change, so the date you saw it matters.
Step by step:
- Go to apprenticeship.gov and open the Apprenticeship Job Finder.
- Type a career path, your city or ZIP code, or both.
- Open a listing and read who the sponsor is, where it is and how to apply.
- Write down the sponsor, job title, location, how to apply and today's date.
- Repeat with another job title until you have two listings.
Words to know:
- Listing: one job or program opening posted on a website.
- Career path: the kind of work you want to do over time, such as electrician or IT support.
- ZIP code: the five-digit number for your area in a US address.
Official sources:
- Apprenticeship.gov: Apprenticeship Job Finder
- Apprenticeship.gov: Career seekers
Try it now: Open the Apprenticeship Job Finder. Search for one career you like near your ZIP code. Write down two listings: sponsor, job title, location, how to apply and today's date. If you find none, try two other job titles or a nearby city.
You can now search the apprenticeship.gov Job Finder and write down two real listings with how to apply.

check.q: You found an apprenticeship on the Job Finder. Who do you apply to?
options: Any website that copies the listing
The employer or sponsor in the listing
check.why: Apprenticeship.gov says you apply directly with the employer or sponsor.

check.q: Your search for "electrician" in your small town shows nothing. What is a good next step?
options: Pay a website to find one for you
Try a nearby bigger city or another job title
check.why: Trying a wider area or other titles often finds listings a first search missed.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Your American Job Center and free training programs
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Find your nearest American Job Center and write the questions you will ask about free training.
This lesson builds toward: Using CareerOneStop or the DOL phone line, you will find your nearest American Job Center and write questions to ask about free training, with at least four questions, including one about training funds.
American Job Centers (AJCs) are free public offices, run with US Department of Labor funds, that help people find jobs and training. Find one on CareerOneStop.org (from the Labor Department) or call the DOL line at 1-877-US-2JOBS (1-877-872-5627). Some states call them by a local name, such as a WorkSource or career center.
Through the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act (WIOA), AJC staff can offer career services and help paying for training if you are eligible. The Labor Department says priority goes to people on public assistance, other low-income people and people who need basic skills help, and veterans get priority of service in all DOL-funded job programs. Services vary by state, so ask.
Other programs to ask about: Job Corps (free training and housing for young adults, generally ages 16 to 24; check jobcorps.gov or call 800-733-5627 for current openings); YouthBuild (ages 16 to 24 who left school without a diploma: construction and other skills while finishing school); Reentry Employment Opportunities for people coming home from prison; and, for veterans, the GI Bill, which the VA says can be used for many apprenticeships and on-the-job training.
Go in with questions written down. You will get more from one visit.
Step by step:
- Search CareerOneStop for American Job Center and your ZIP code, or call 1-877-US-2JOBS.
- Write down the center's address, hours and phone number.
- Write your questions: training funds, programs near you, apprenticeships, help for your situation.
- Call or visit and take notes, including the name of the person you talk to.
Words to know:
- American Job Center (AJC): a free public office that helps people find jobs and training.
- WIOA: the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act, the US law that funds job centers and training help.
- Eligible: meeting the rules to get a service.
- Priority of service: being served first; veterans get it in DOL-funded job programs.
- GI Bill: VA education benefits for veterans and some family members.
Official sources:
- US Department of Labor: WIOA Adult program
- CareerOneStop: Find an American Job Center
- Job Corps
- US Department of Labor: YouthBuild
- US Department of Labor: Youth and reentry programs
- VA: On-the-job training and apprenticeships
Try it now: Find your nearest American Job Center and write its address, hours and phone. Then write four questions to ask, for example: "Can WIOA help pay for training in my field?", "Which apprenticeships or pre-apprenticeships are near here?", "Is there help for young adults, veterans or people with a record?", "What do I bring to my first visit?"
You can now find your American Job Center and go in with questions about free training and programs.

check.q: Where can you get free help finding training money and programs near you?
options: A company that charges to place you
check.why: American Job Centers are free public offices that help with jobs and training, including WIOA funds.

check.q: Which question is best to ask at an American Job Center?
options: "Can you do my job for me?"
"Can WIOA help pay for training in my field?"
check.why: Asking about WIOA training funds can open free training if you are eligible.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Is the program real and worth it?
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check a program ad for the signs that it is real, and for the signs of a scam.
This lesson builds toward: Given a program ad or offer, you will check whether the program is real and worth your time, using at least three checks, including the warning signs of a pay-to-get-a-job scam.
Some ads promise "guaranteed jobs" if you pay for training or a certificate. The FTC says honest employers, including the federal government, will never ask you to pay to get a job, and paying for useless "training" or certifications is a common scam.
Other FTC warning signs: a check you must deposit and then send part of the money back, an upfront fee from a placement firm, a stranger who contacts you out of the blue with a job, and big pay for little work.
Signs a program is real: it is listed on apprenticeship.gov, your American Job Center, a state .gov site, a union or a community college; you can find its address and phone on its own; and it tells you clearly what it costs, how long it takes, what credential you get, and how many people finish and get jobs.
A real program can still be a poor fit. Check the schedule, the location and travel, and whether the credential is one employers in your area ask for.
Step by step:
- Look for the program on an official site (apprenticeship.gov, your AJC, a state .gov site, a union or college).
- Find its address and phone yourself; do not use only the number in the ad.
- Check for scam signs: paying to get the job, upfront fees, check-and-send-back, too-good pay.
- Ask: cost, length, credential, schedule, and how many finish and get jobs.
- Not sure? Ask your American Job Center before you sign or pay anything.
Words to know:
- Scam: a trick to take your money or personal information.
- Upfront fee: money you must pay before you get anything.
- FTC: the Federal Trade Commission, the US agency that warns about and fights scams.
- Completion rate: how many people who start a program finish it.
Official sources:
- FTC: Job scams
- Apprenticeship.gov: Apprenticeship Job Finder
Try it now: Take one program you found in Lesson 2 or 3. Do three checks: is it on an official list, can you find its address and phone yourself, and does it show any scam sign? Write "real", "not sure" or "scam" and why. Then read this made-up ad and list its warning signs: "Get a guaranteed $40/hour job! Pay $300 today for your certificate. Text us now."
You can now check whether a program is real and worth your time, and spot the signs of a pay-to-get-a-job scam.

check.q: An ad says: "Pay $250 for your certificate and get a guaranteed job." What do you do?
options: Pay quickly before it fills up
Send your bank details to hold a spot
Treat it as a likely scam and check with your AJC
Share it with friends so they pay too
check.why: The FTC says honest employers never ask you to pay to get a job.

check.q: Which is a sign a program is real?
options: It is listed on apprenticeship.gov or a state .gov site
It only has a phone number in a text
It asks you to deposit a check and send money back
It will not tell you what it costs
check.why: Being listed on an official site and being open about costs are signs of a real program.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Requirements and documents
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List a program's requirements and the documents you need, and mark which you have.
This lesson builds toward: For one program you want, you will list its requirements and the documents you need to apply, marking which ones you already have and where to get the rest.
Every program sets its own requirements, and they are in the listing or on the sponsor's site. Common ones are a minimum age, a high school diploma or equivalency (GED or HiSET), a basic math or reading test, being able to do the physical work, a valid driver's license for some trades, and a drug test.
Common documents: a photo ID, proof of your diploma or equivalency, school transcripts, a résumé, and sometimes a Social Security card or proof you can work in the US. Veterans may need their DD-214 to show their service, and GI Bill users apply for VA education benefits.
Do not have one yet? You can still plan. A state ID comes from your state's DMV. A diploma copy comes from your old school or state education office. The American Job Center can help with many of these, and reentry programs often help people coming home get ID.
Keep copies, not originals, in one folder. Never send private numbers to anyone you have not checked is real.
Step by step:
- Open the listing or the sponsor's page and find the requirements.
- Write each requirement and each document on a checklist.
- Mark each one: Have it, Need it, or Not sure.
- Next to each Need it, write where you will get it.
- Put copies in one folder or a safe place on your phone.
Words to know:
- Requirement: something you must have or do to apply, such as a minimum age or a diploma.
- Equivalency: a test, such as the GED or HiSET, that counts like a high school diploma.
- Transcript: the official list of classes and grades from a school.
- DD-214: the military paper that shows a veteran's service and discharge.
Official sources:
- Apprenticeship.gov: Career seekers
- VA: On-the-job training and apprenticeships
Try it now: For one program you want, make a checklist of every requirement and document from its listing. Mark each one Have it, Need it or Not sure, and write where you will get each Need it. Do not write any real ID numbers on the list.
You can now list a program's requirements and documents, see what you are missing and know where to get it.

check.q: Where do you find a program's exact requirements?
options: The program's listing or the sponsor's own site
They are the same for every program
check.why: Each program sets its own requirements, so you read its listing or official page.

check.q: Luis, a veteran, wants to use the GI Bill for an apprenticeship. Which document will likely help show his service?
check.why: The DD-214 shows a veteran's service and discharge.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Making your application plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write an application plan for two programs with dated steps and a follow-up date.
This lesson builds toward: For two programs you found, you will write an application plan with dated next steps, with at least five steps, deadlines and a follow-up date.
Apprenticeships and training programs often open applications only at certain times, and some fill fast. A written plan with dates keeps you from missing a window.
For each program, write the deadline or the next open date, how to apply (online, in person, or at an information session), and any test date. If you cannot find a date, your first step is to call or email and ask.
Then write your next steps, each with a date: get a missing document, update your résumé, practice for the math test, go to an information session, submit the application, follow up. A good follow-up is a short, polite call or email about one to two weeks after you apply, unless the program tells you a different time.
Apply to more than one program. If one says no or puts you on a waiting list, you still have another path, and you can ask what would make you a stronger applicant next time.
Step by step:
- Choose two programs you checked are real.
- Write each one's deadline or next open date and how to apply.
- List your next steps, with a date for each.
- Put the dates in your phone calendar or on paper you see every day.
- Set a follow-up date after you apply.
Words to know:
- Deadline: the last day you can apply.
- Information session: a meeting where a program explains how it works and how to apply.
- Waiting list: a list of people who will get a place if one opens.
- Follow up: contact a program after you apply to check on your application.
Official sources:
- Apprenticeship.gov: Apprenticeship Job Finder
- US Department of Labor: WIOA Adult program
Try it now: Make your Program Application Plan: your goal job, two checked programs with deadlines and how to apply, your document checklist, and five next steps with dates, ending with a follow-up date. Put the first step's date in your phone or calendar today.
You can now write an application plan with dated steps for two programs and follow up after you apply.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Right kind of program The plan does not say whether each program is an apprenticeship, a pre-apprenticeship or a training program. Each program is named as the right kind, and the learner can say why it fits now. The plan also says what the learner would do next after finishing it (for example, pre-apprenticeship then apprenticeship). Two real programs found Fewer than two programs, or a program with no sponsor, location or way to apply. Two programs with sponsor, location and how to apply, from apprenticeship.gov, an AJC or another official source. Also notes the date each was found and a backup program. Job center questions No American Job Center or questions listed. The nearest AJC and at least four questions, including one about training funds. The learner called or visited and wrote down the answers and the staff person's name. Programs checked No checks shown, or a program that asks for a fee to get the job. At least three checks per program, including scam warning signs, with a result. Also compares cost, length, credential and job results for the two programs. Documents ready No document list, or real ID numbers written on it. Requirements and documents marked Have it / Need it, with where to get each missing item. All missing items have a date to get them. Dated plan Steps have no dates, or there are fewer than five. Five or more steps with dates, deadlines and a follow-up date. The first step is already done or on the learner's calendar. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: You cannot find a program's application deadline. What is your first step?
options: Call or email the program and ask
Apply to a random program instead
check.why: Asking the program directly gets you the real date for your plan.

check.q: Why apply to two programs instead of one?
options: So you still have a path if one says no or waitlists you
So you can skip the deadlines
check.why: A second program keeps you moving if the first does not work out.
